resources.title: Abert's squirrel
resources.description: Identify Abert's squirrel, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Abert's squirrel (Sciurus aberti): Long, pointed ear tufts (tassels) on the ears. Gray-and-white coloring. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Colorado Plateau and southern Rocky Mountains of Colorado, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico, south into Mexico's Sierra Madre Occidental; not in Canada. Transplanted populations are established in Arizona's Graham and Santa Catalina mountains.

rangeSummary.value: Colorado Plateau and southern Rocky Mountains of Colorado, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico, south into Mexico's Sierra Madre Occidental; not in Canada. Transplanted populations are established in Arizona's Graham and Santa Catalina mountains.

identification.text: Long, pointed ear tufts (tassels) on the ears.
Gray-and-white coloring.
The Kaibab squirrel (S. a. kaibabensis) is one of nine subspecies and was formerly treated as a separate species.

habitat.text: Nearly confined to cool, dry ponderosa pine forest, typically between 5,500 and 8,500 ft elevation; optimum habitat is all-aged ponderosa pine stands.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Diurnal and active year-round.
Feeds on ponderosa pine seeds (preferred), inner bark of young twigs, buds and fungi; in winter clips roughly 45 twigs a day, leaving clipped twigs under pines.
Builds nests of pine twigs high in the crown (about 16–90 ft up), usually on the south side of the tree.
Summer home ranges average about 18 acres; winter ranges are smaller.

resources.title: American badger
resources.description: Identify American badger, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American badger (Taxidea taxus): Heavy, flattened body with short stocky legs, short neck, broad head and short bushy tail; 26-35 in long, roughly 4-12 kg. Very long front claws. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Primarily the Great Plains: north into the central-western Canadian provinces, through suitable habitat across the western United States and south into Mexico; has expanded east since about 1900 and now reaches Ontario.

rangeSummary.value: Primarily the Great Plains: north into the central-western Canadian provinces, through suitable habitat across the western United States and south into Mexico; has expanded east since about 1900 and now reaches Ontario.

identification.text: Heavy, flattened body with short stocky legs, short neck, broad head and short bushy tail; 26-35 in long, roughly 4-12 kg.
Very long front claws.
Brown face marked with a white stripe running back from the nose, white patches and vertical black bars; throat and chin whitish.
The white head stripe ends near the shoulders in northern animals but runs to the rump in southern ones.
Grayish to reddish back and flanks with a buffy belly; low, rounded ears.

habitat.text: Dry, open grasslands, prairies, fields and pastures, favouring sandy soils where burrowing prey is easy to dig out; from alpine meadows to below sea level.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Solitary and mainly nocturnal; less active in winter, passing it in bouts of torpor and emerging on warm days.
Catches most food by digging after pocket gophers, ground squirrels, prairie dogs, mice and voles; also eats rabbits, insects, reptiles and eggs.
Digs a series of dens across its home range; typical burrows are about 1 ft in diameter, leaving conspicuous holes and mounds.

resources.title: American bison
resources.description: Identify American bison, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American bison (Bison bison): Largest land mammal in North America; bulls about 900 kg, cows about 500 kg. Dark chocolate-brown with long hair on the head, shoulders and forelegs and short hair on the flanks and hindquarters. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Once widespread from Alaska and western Canada across the U.S. into northern Mexico; now in isolated herds within and outside the historical range. Yellowstone is the only place in the lower 48 states with a continuously free-ranging population since prehistoric times.

rangeSummary.value: Once widespread from Alaska and western Canada across the U.S. into northern Mexico; now in isolated herds within and outside the historical range. Yellowstone is the only place in the lower 48 states with a continuously free-ranging population since prehistoric times.

identification.text: Largest land mammal in North America; bulls about 900 kg, cows about 500 kg.
Dark chocolate-brown with long hair on the head, shoulders and forelegs and short hair on the flanks and hindquarters.
Protruding shoulder hump.
Both sexes carry short, upward-curving horns.
Calves are reddish-tan at birth and begin turning brown after about 2.5 months.

habitat.text: Open plains and grasslands in the south; boreal forest openings, meadows and river valleys in the north; attracted to recently burned areas.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Herds of cows and young appear to be led by older females; groups average about 20 in winter and about 200 in summer
Rut in July and August: bulls bellow, wallow and fight
Grazes grasses and sedges 9–11 hours a day; swings its head to clear snow
Rubs on trees and rocks and uses dirt wallows

resources.title: Axis deer
resources.description: Identify Axis deer, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Axis deer (Axis axis): Yellowish-brown to rufous coat profusely dappled with white spots year-round. White abdomen, rump, throat, inner legs and underside of tail; dark stripe from nape nearly to tail tip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to India, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Introduced into Texas about 1932, where more than 15,000 are free-living in central and southern counties; also established in Hawaii and Florida.

rangeSummary.value: Native to India, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Introduced into Texas about 1932, where more than 15,000 are free-living in central and southern counties; also established in Hawaii and Florida.

identification.text: Yellowish-brown to rufous coat profusely dappled with white spots year-round.
White abdomen, rump, throat, inner legs and underside of tail; dark stripe from nape nearly to tail tip.
Males carry three-tined antlers; the brow tine forms nearly a right angle with the beam.
Females smaller and usually antlerless; males 30–75 kg.

habitat.text: Secondary forest broken by grassy glades with water and shade; avoids rugged terrain; grazes short green grass and sedges, supplemented by browse.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Gregarious; herds range from a few animals to over 100, usually led by an old doe
Adult males normally live in mixed herds, unlike native deer
Rutting males give bugle-like bellows; both sexes bark in alarm
Bucks in hard antler and rut can be found in any month; main breeding mid-May to August, most Texas fawns born January to mid-April

resources.title: Barbary sheep
resources.description: Identify Barbary sheep, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia): Rufous or grayish-brown above with a blackish stripe down the back; whitish belly and inner legs. Long hair on the throat, chest and front legs; no beard. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to North Africa. Introduced to New Mexico (1950) and Texas (Palo Duro Canyon, 1957–1958) and now established in the Texas Panhandle canyons, Trans-Pecos and Edwards Plateau.

rangeSummary.value: Native to North Africa. Introduced to New Mexico (1950) and Texas (Palo Duro Canyon, 1957–1958) and now established in the Texas Panhandle canyons, Trans-Pecos and Edwards Plateau.

identification.text: Rufous or grayish-brown above with a blackish stripe down the back; whitish belly and inner legs.
Long hair on the throat, chest and front legs; no beard.
Horns curve outward, backward and then inward, with transverse wrinkles; yellowish-brown, darkening with age.
Females are much smaller (to about 65 kg) with smaller horns; males reach about 145 kg.
Compared with the bighorn sheep: Aoudad have long hair on the throat, chest and forelegs; they share similar terrain and may compete with bighorns.

habitat.text: Dry, rough, barren and largely waterless rocky terrain, similar to desert bighorn sheep country.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Lives in small mixed-sex groups and climbs steep slopes expertly.
Eats browse, grasses and forbs (one study: 49% browse, 42% grass, 9% forbs) and can survive without free water.
Breeding peaks mid-September to mid-November; lambs born late February through April.

resources.title: Bighorn sheep
resources.description: Identify Bighorn sheep, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis): Rams carry massive, curling horns that can weigh up to 14 kg; ewes have much smaller, only slightly curved horns. Rams 119-127 kg; ewes 53-91 kg. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Rocky Mountains from southern Canada to Colorado; desert bighorn from Nevada and California to west Texas and into Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: Rocky Mountains from southern Canada to Colorado; desert bighorn from Nevada and California to west Texas and into Mexico.

identification.text: Rams carry massive, curling horns that can weigh up to 14 kg; ewes have much smaller, only slightly curved horns.
Rams 119-127 kg; ewes 53-91 kg.
Summer coat rich glossy brown, fading by late winter.
The desert subspecies is somewhat smaller with flatter, wider-spreading horns.

habitat.text: Alpine meadows, grassy mountain slopes and foothills close to rugged cliffs and bluffs, on drier slopes with limited snowfall. Winter range is typically about 760-1,520 m and summer range 1,830-2,590 m elevation.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Gregarious: small groups of 8-10 are common, occasionally herds of over 100; mature rams live apart in bachelor groups most of the year.
Most populations move seasonally, using larger upland areas in summer and sheltered valleys in winter.
Mainly daytime feeders and largely grazers on grasses, sedges and forbs, taking browse when preferred foods are scarce.
Keen-sighted and able to spot movement up to about 1.6 km away; moves with ease on cliff ledges.

conservationStatus.text: peninsular bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis nelsoni), U.S.A. (CA) Peninsular Ranges: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1998-03-18.
Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis sierrae), U.S.A. (CA) Sierra Nevada: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1999-04-20.

resources.title: Black-tailed jackrabbit
resources.description: Identify Black-tailed jackrabbit, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus): Lanky hare, 47-63 cm long, with very long ears (10-13 cm) and long hind legs. Black stripe down the centre of the back, a black rump patch, and a tail black on top. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern United States and Mexico, east to Missouri and north to Washington, Idaho, Colorado and Nebraska, west to California and Baja California.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern United States and Mexico, east to Missouri and north to Washington, Idaho, Colorado and Nebraska, west to California and Baja California.

identification.text: Lanky hare, 47-63 cm long, with very long ears (10-13 cm) and long hind legs.
Black stripe down the centre of the back, a black rump patch, and a tail black on top.
Sexes look alike; females larger.
Compared with the white-tailed jackrabbit: White-tailed jackrabbit's tail is always white, without the black tail top and back stripe.
Compared with the eastern cottontail: Cottontails are smaller with shorter ears and legs; jackrabbits have ears, hind legs and feet very large in proportion to the body.

habitat.text: Desert scrub, prairie, short-grass rangeland, dunes and farmland from sea level to about 3,800 m.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal; rests by day in shallow scraped depressions ('forms') under bushes and is inactive in hot afternoons.
Relies on freezing and speed: flushes in bounds up to 20 ft, reaching 30-35 mph on a zigzag course.
Eats grasses and herbs, turning to twigs, bark, sagebrush and cacti when other food is short; gets most water from plants.

resources.title: Brush rabbit
resources.description: Identify Brush rabbit, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Brush rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani): Small to medium cottontail, 28–37 cm long; females slightly larger than males. Evenly dark coat of steel gray, black and orange above, white below. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Pacific coast from the Columbia River (Oregon–Washington border) south, west of the Cascades, Sierra Nevada and deserts, through much of California to Baja California. In Oregon it occupies the Willamette and other interior valleys and the coast.

rangeSummary.value: Pacific coast from the Columbia River (Oregon–Washington border) south, west of the Cascades, Sierra Nevada and deserts, through much of California to Baja California. In Oregon it occupies the Willamette and other interior valleys and the coast.

identification.text: Small to medium cottontail, 28–37 cm long; females slightly larger than males.
Evenly dark coat of steel gray, black and orange above, white below.
Fairly small ears with a slight point.
Tail not prominent.

habitat.text: Dense scrub, chaparral, bramble thickets and brushy edges, including brush on sand dunes; seldom uses burrows.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Mainly crepuscular: emerges after sunset and is active into early morning, rarely in the afternoon
Rarely goes more than a few metres from dense brush, using cleared runways into grassy feeding areas
Thumps its feet when frightened, freezes for long periods, and flees in a zig-zag; may climb into shrubs when pursued

conservationStatus.text: riparian brush rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani riparius): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2000-02-23.

resources.title: Collared peccary
resources.description: Identify Collared peccary, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Collared peccary (Pecari tajacu): Pig-like; grizzled black and gray with a dark stripe down the back. Whitish collar across the shoulders in adults. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Arizona, New Mexico and western and southern Texas, south through Mexico to Argentina; not in Canada. Introduced populations exist in north-central Texas.

rangeSummary.value: Arizona, New Mexico and western and southern Texas, south through Mexico to Argentina; not in Canada. Introduced populations exist in north-central Texas.

identification.text: Pig-like; grizzled black and gray with a dark stripe down the back.
Whitish collar across the shoulders in adults.
Young are reddish to yellowish brown with a black back stripe.
Musk (scent) gland on the rump; adults about 35–55 lb.
Compared with the feral hog: Peccaries are native New World animals, whereas pigs are Old World species introduced from Europe; the peccary shows a whitish shoulder collar.

habitat.text: Brushy semidesert where prickly pear is conspicuous; dense thickets, rocky canyons, chaparral and scrub oak. In Arizona from desert floor to about 7,000 ft, usually below 5,500 ft.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Lives in herds of a few to several dozen animals.
Mainly active early morning and late afternoon, somewhat nocturnal; huddles on cool nights.
Eats prickly pear and other succulents, roots, fruits, nuts and mesquite beans; leaves shredded cactus pads and uprooted plants.
Communicates with grunts, growls and tooth 'pops'; very poor eyesight but a keen sense of smell.

resources.title: Dall sheep
resources.description: Identify Dall sheep, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Dall sheep (Ovis dalli): White wild sheep. Rams carry massive curled horns; ewes have shorter, slender, slightly curved horns. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Brooks Range, Alaska Range and Kenai Peninsula of Alaska, and the Mackenzie and northern Rocky Mountains of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and northern British Columbia; many southern populations are isolated.

rangeSummary.value: Brooks Range, Alaska Range and Kenai Peninsula of Alaska, and the Mackenzie and northern Rocky Mountains of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and northern British Columbia; many southern populations are isolated.

identification.text: White wild sheep.
Rams carry massive curled horns; ewes have shorter, slender, slightly curved horns.
Rams under about 3 years resemble ewes; yearling rams are hard to tell from ewes.
Horn growth rings (annuli) indicate age.
Compared with the mountain goat: Sometimes confused; Dall sheep prefer drier country and do not occur in Southeast Alaska.

habitat.text: Relatively dry mountain country: open alpine ridges, meadows and steep slopes next to rugged cliffs used as escape terrain.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Rams live in bands apart from ewe groups except during the late November–early December rut
Rams clash horns to establish rank
Moves to higher elevations in spring and lower in fall; very loyal to seasonal home ranges
Travels many miles to mineral licks in spring

resources.title: Desert cottontail
resources.description: Identify Desert cottontail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Desert cottontail (Sylvilagus audubonii): Medium cottontail, total length about 38 cm and roughly 0.8-1 kg; females slightly larger than males. Bushy white 'cotton' tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern North America from northern Montana south to central Mexico and west to the Pacific coast.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern North America from northern Montana south to central Mexico and west to the Pacific coast.

identification.text: Medium cottontail, total length about 38 cm and roughly 0.8-1 kg; females slightly larger than males.
Bushy white 'cotton' tail.
Long ears (about 7 cm) and hind feet about 9 cm.

habitat.text: Mainly arid regions, but also woodland and grassland from sea level to about 1,800 m; shelters in heavy brush, brambles or holes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Most active in early morning and evening, spending the rest of the day under cover.
Not gregarious; home range generally about 3 ha (8 acres).
When startled it freezes or runs for cover in a zig-zag at about 24 km/h; can swim and climb brush piles.
Eats almost exclusively grasses, plus some fruit, nuts and vegetables.

resources.title: Fallow deer
resources.description: Identify Fallow deer, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Fallow deer (Dama dama): Medium, rangy deer standing 91–97 cm at the shoulder. Mature bucks (3–4 years and older) carry broad palmate antlers; younger bucks have simple beams and points. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to the Mediterranean and Asia Minor. Introduced in North America: Texas has over 10,000 (about a third free-ranging), with other introduced or semi-wild populations in several U.S. states and on western Canadian islands in British Columbia.

rangeSummary.value: Native to the Mediterranean and Asia Minor. Introduced in North America: Texas has over 10,000 (about a third free-ranging), with other introduced or semi-wild populations in several U.S. states and on western Canadian islands in British Columbia.

identification.text: Medium, rangy deer standing 91–97 cm at the shoulder.
Mature bucks (3–4 years and older) carry broad palmate antlers; younger bucks have simple beams and points.
Four colour forms: common (rust with white spots, fading in winter), menil (tan, spots distinct in winter), white (dark eyes) and black.
Black line down the back often joins the black upper tail in the common form.

habitat.text: Feeds in open grassy areas but needs tree cover and undergrowth; deciduous or mixed woodland on gently rolling terrain is best.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Rut mid-September into November, peaking in October; bucks defend a small 'stand'
After the rut males form bachelor groups while does and young stay separate
Feeds as a grazer or browser depending on competition with livestock and white-tailed deer

resources.title: Fox squirrel
resources.description: Identify Fox squirrel, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Fox squirrel (Sciurus niger): Heavy-bodied tree squirrel, 19-29 in and 1-3 lb, larger than the gray squirrel. Back and sides reddish yellow mixed with gray; belly and tail fringe reddish yellow to orange. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central United States, north into Canada and south into northern Mexico; introduced into urban areas of western North America.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central United States, north into Canada and south into northern Mexico; introduced into urban areas of western North America.

identification.text: Heavy-bodied tree squirrel, 19-29 in and 1-3 lb, larger than the gray squirrel.
Back and sides reddish yellow mixed with gray; belly and tail fringe reddish yellow to orange.
Black individuals occur, notably in some southeastern populations.
Ear tufts often develop in winter.
Compared with the eastern gray squirrel: Gray squirrel is slimmer and smaller with a gray back and white belly and tail fringe.

habitat.text: Deciduous and mixed forest with varied mast trees, often on ridges, farm woodlots, timbered fence rows and hedgerows in prairie country, and towns with large oaks and hickories.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Active by day and mostly in trees; generally solitary except during mating chases.
Barks and chatters; threatens with an upright stance and tail flicks.
Prefers acorns, hickory nuts, walnuts, mulberry and hawthorn seeds, and scatter-caches nuts for winter.
Nests in tree cavities or bulky leaf nests averaging about 40 ft up.

resources.title: Mountain cottontail
resources.description: Identify Mountain cottontail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Mountain cottontail (Sylvilagus nuttallii): Medium to large cottontail, 35-39 cm, 0.7-1.2 kg, with long hind legs. Greyish-brown upperparts, white belly; tail large, dark above and light below. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mostly the western United States from the Sierra Nevada east to Montana's eastern border and south to central New Mexico and Arizona, reaching into a small area of southern Canada north of Montana and Washington.

rangeSummary.value: Mostly the western United States from the Sierra Nevada east to Montana's eastern border and south to central New Mexico and Arizona, reaching into a small area of southern Canada north of Montana and Washington.

identification.text: Medium to large cottontail, 35-39 cm, 0.7-1.2 kg, with long hind legs.
Greyish-brown upperparts, white belly; tail large, dark above and light below.
Hind legs covered with long, dense reddish-brown hair.
Short, rounded ears with black tips and long hairs on the inner surfaces.

habitat.text: Brushy or wooded slopes and riverbanks with grasses, willows and especially sagebrush; on sparse rocky slopes it hides in burrows or rock crevices.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Solitary and crepuscular, feeding in or near sheltering brush; active year-round.
When frightened, runs a few metres to cover and freezes with ears erect before hopping away.
Prefers grasses; when grass is scarce eats sagebrush and western juniper.

resources.title: Mountain goat
resources.description: Identify Mountain goat, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Mountain goat (Oreamnos americanus): White coat, long and shaggy in winter, with a crest of erect hair along the spine and rump and long leg hair ('pantaloons'). Both sexes have short, black horns that are never shed and grow annual rings. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from southeast Alaska through western Canada to Washington, western Montana and central Idaho. Introduced populations exist in South Dakota, Colorado, Washington and on several Alaskan islands.

rangeSummary.value: Native from southeast Alaska through western Canada to Washington, western Montana and central Idaho. Introduced populations exist in South Dakota, Colorado, Washington and on several Alaskan islands.

identification.text: White coat, long and shaggy in winter, with a crest of erect hair along the spine and rump and long leg hair ('pantaloons').
Both sexes have short, black horns that are never shed and grow annual rings.
Females' horns are more slender and bend back sharply; males' horns are more evenly curved.
Males are markedly larger than females (Alaska: about 280 lb vs 180 lb).
Compared with the dall sheep: Dall sheep are also white but lack the mountain goat's black horns and prefer drier country.

habitat.text: Steep, rocky cliffs and bluffs in alpine and subalpine terrain.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Nannies form nursery groups with kids and young; billies stay in small bachelor groups except during the late October–early December rut.
Active from sunrise to mid-day and again at dusk; digs shallow beds for resting and dust bathing.
Grazes sedges, forbs and low shrubs in alpine meadows in summer; browses in winter.
Moves from alpine summer range to treeline or old-growth forest in winter.

resources.title: Mountain lion
resources.description: Identify Mountain lion, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Mountain lion (Puma concolor): Very large, slender cat with a small head and small rounded ears without tufts. Uniform grizzled gray to tawny, cinnamon or rufous upperparts; whitish underparts, chin and throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Historically ranged coast to coast in North America and north to southeastern Alaska. Now largely restricted to mountainous, sparsely populated areas, expanding in the western United States; eastern populations were exterminated except a small Florida panther population. Lions confirmed farther east, such as in Missouri, are likely wanderers from the west, and eastern sightings outside Florida are often escaped captive cats.

rangeSummary.value: Historically ranged coast to coast in North America and north to southeastern Alaska. Now largely restricted to mountainous, sparsely populated areas, expanding in the western United States; eastern populations were exterminated except a small Florida panther population. Lions confirmed farther east, such as in Missouri, are likely wanderers from the west, and eastern sightings outside Florida are often escaped captive cats.

identification.text: Very large, slender cat with a small head and small rounded ears without tufts.
Uniform grizzled gray to tawny, cinnamon or rufous upperparts; whitish underparts, chin and throat.
Long, heavy, cylindrical tail about one-third of total length, with the last 2-3 in black.
Black sides of the muzzle and black behind the ears; pinkish nose.
Males 79-265 lb, females 64-141 lb; total length 5-8.5 ft.
Compared with the bobcat: Bobcat is much smaller with a short tail and a spotted, streaked coat rather than uniform colour.

habitat.text: Areas with dense cover or rocky, rugged terrain and low human population, from mountain conifer forest to grassland, brush country and swamps.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Solitary and primarily nocturnal, though sometimes active by day; climbs trees readily.
Ambush predator that stalks and attacks at close range; deer are the main prey, also elk and smaller mammals.
Caches large kills under leaves and debris, dragging them up to 350 m, and returns nightly to feed.
Marks territory with scrapes, urine and scat; vocalizations include hisses, growls, yowls and screams.

conservationStatus.text: Florida panther (Puma  concolor coryi): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Muskox
resources.description: Identify Muskox, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Muskox (Ovibos moschatus): Stocky, short-legged animal with a slight shoulder hump, very short tail and long guard hair hanging nearly to the ground. Dark brown coat with creamy hair on the saddle, forehead and legs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native populations in North America occur only in northern Canada, mostly on the Arctic islands (especially Banks and Victoria), with a mainland population north of Great Bear Lake, around Queen Maud Gulf and in northeastern Keewatin. Introduced free-ranging population in Quebec; reintroduced to Alaska from Greenland stock in 1930 (Nunivak Island, later Seward Peninsula and elsewhere).

rangeSummary.value: Native populations in North America occur only in northern Canada, mostly on the Arctic islands (especially Banks and Victoria), with a mainland population north of Great Bear Lake, around Queen Maud Gulf and in northeastern Keewatin. Introduced free-ranging population in Quebec; reintroduced to Alaska from Greenland stock in 1930 (Nunivak Island, later Seward Peninsula and elsewhere).

identification.text: Stocky, short-legged animal with a slight shoulder hump, very short tail and long guard hair hanging nearly to the ground.
Dark brown coat with creamy hair on the saddle, forehead and legs.
Both sexes have horns that curve down beside the face and up at the tips; on bulls the bases form a solid boss across the forehead, while cows have a fur patch between the horn bases.
Bulls about 5 ft at the shoulder and 600-800 lb (Alaska data); cows smaller.
In midsummer the woolly undercoat (qiviut) sheds, leaving animals shaggy and ragged for weeks.

habitat.text: Low-lying coastal and inland plains and river valleys of the Arctic where shrubs are most abundant.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Winter herds may hold up to 75 animals; herds break into small groups around calving.
Rut August-October: bulls give deep, rumbling roar-like bellows and charge head-on, clashing horn bosses repeatedly.
Eats grasses, sedges, forbs and woody plants; poorly adapted to digging through heavy snow, so winter range is limited to areas of shallow snow.
Endures severe storms lying down with its back to the wind.

resources.title: Muskrat
resources.description: Identify Muskrat, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus): Rotund rodent 26–36 cm plus a 20–28 cm scaly, rat-like tail; 0.9–1.8 kg. Silvery to dark brown glossy coat with a lighter belly; dark feet and tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: North America north to the treeline, including Newfoundland, south to the Gulf Coast, Rio Grande and lower Colorado River; introduced in Eurasia and Argentina.

rangeSummary.value: North America north to the treeline, including Newfoundland, south to the Gulf Coast, Rio Grande and lower Colorado River; introduced in Eurasia and Argentina.

identification.text: Rotund rodent 26–36 cm plus a 20–28 cm scaly, rat-like tail; 0.9–1.8 kg.
Silvery to dark brown glossy coat with a lighter belly; dark feet and tail.
Hind feet large but not webbed, fringed with stiff hairs.
Compared with the beaver: The muskrat is much smaller with a rat-like tail rather than a broad flat one.
Compared with the nutria: Nutria are much larger with a round tail and white whiskers; muskrats have a side-flattened tail and no webbing between the toes.

habitat.text: Freshwater marshes, marshy lake edges and slow streams with water deep enough not to freeze to the bottom but shallow enough for aquatic plants (ideally 1–2 m).

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Builds dome houses of cattail and bulrush 0.6–0.9 m high, or tunnels into banks
In winter feeds under the ice and builds 'pushups' of vegetation over holes
Mainly eats roots and stems of cattails, lilies, sedges and grasses; occasionally mussels and small fish
Leaves musky scent at stations and makes slides and channels through bank vegetation

resources.title: New England cottontail
resources.description: Identify New England cottontail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: New England cottontail (Sylvilagus transitionalis): Grayish-brown rabbit nearly identical to the eastern cottontail. Shorter ears, a black spot between the ears and a black line on the front edge of the ears. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native only to New England and eastern New York; in New York now confined to Columbia, Dutchess, Putnam and Westchester counties east of the Hudson. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Native only to New England and eastern New York; in New York now confined to Columbia, Dutchess, Putnam and Westchester counties east of the Hudson. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Grayish-brown rabbit nearly identical to the eastern cottontail.
Shorter ears, a black spot between the ears and a black line on the front edge of the ears.
Lacks the white forehead spot shown by many eastern cottontails.
Field marks are unreliable; certain identification needs skull examination or DNA (e.g., from fecal pellets).
Compared with the eastern cottontail: Eastern cottontails often show a white forehead spot and have longer ears without a black front edge, but only DNA or skulls are certain.

habitat.text: Early-successional thickets, shrubby areas and shrub wetlands with some canopy cover and native shrubs.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Hides in dense cover by day; most active at dawn and dusk.
Summer diet of grasses and herbaceous plants; autumn and winter diet of bark, twigs and buds of blackberry, raspberry, blueberry and willow.
Home ranges from half an acre to eight acres; males range more widely.

resources.title: Nilgai
resources.description: Identify Nilgai, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus): Among the largest Asian antelopes: 120-150 cm at the shoulder, stocky body on slender legs. Adult males blue-gray; females and young yellow-brown to pale brown. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Introduced: native to India; released on South Texas ranches around 1930. Most are on large ranches in Kenedy and Willacy counties, Texas.

rangeSummary.value: Introduced: native to India; released on South Texas ranches around 1930. Most are on large ranches in Kenedy and Willacy counties, Texas.

identification.text: Among the largest Asian antelopes: 120-150 cm at the shoulder, stocky body on slender legs.
Adult males blue-gray; females and young yellow-brown to pale brown.
White patches on the face and below the chin and a broad white throat 'bib'; males have a hanging throat tuft up to 13 cm.
Males carry short black horns about 20-25 cm.
White band from the brisket over the belly forming a narrow rump patch outlined in darker hair.

habitat.text: In Texas, South Texas brush country; native habitat is dry grassland, steppe woodland and hillsides in India.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Usually in herds of about 10, sometimes 20-70.
Most active in early morning and late afternoon.
Eyesight and hearing equal to or better than white-tailed deer, but a poor sense of smell; spooks easily and can run up to 29 mph.
Grazes and browses; in Texas eats mesquite, oak, partridge pea, croton, nightshade and grasses.

resources.title: North American river otter
resources.description: Identify North American river otter, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: North American river otter (Lontra canadensis): Thickset, 102–152 cm long, 6.8–15 kg, with short legs and a neck as thick as the head. Inconspicuous ears; thick, tapered tail about a third of body length. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Throughout most of North America north of Mexico except the extreme southwestern U.S.; extirpated from large areas of the interior U.S. and reintroduced in some states.

rangeSummary.value: Throughout most of North America north of Mexico except the extreme southwestern U.S.; extirpated from large areas of the interior U.S. and reintroduced in some states.

identification.text: Thickset, 102–152 cm long, 6.8–15 kg, with short legs and a neck as thick as the head.
Inconspicuous ears; thick, tapered tail about a third of body length.
Only the hind feet are webbed.
Prime fur black-brown with a slightly paler belly and grayish chin and throat.

habitat.text: Streams, lakes, ponds, swamps, marshes, beaver flowages, estuaries and exposed Pacific coastline; dens in abandoned beaver lodges, burrows, log jams and thickets near water.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Signs are seen more often than the animal: well-used overland trails between waters, rolling areas, twisted grass tufts and scent-post scats
Runs and slides on snow and ice, and slides on mud
Eats fish, mollusks, crabs, frogs and other aquatic prey; small items eaten at the surface, larger ones ashore
Travels in family groups or bachelor-male groups over large, overlapping, usually linear home ranges

resources.title: Nutria
resources.description: Identify Nutria, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Nutria (Myocastor coypus): Large semi-aquatic rodent, body 47–61 cm plus a 37–41 cm tail; up to about 9 kg. Light to dark brown fur; long, round, sparsely haired tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to southern South America. Introduced in Louisiana in the 1930s and spread widely; now in the southeastern and south-central U.S., Oregon, Washington, Maryland and other states, with records in British Columbia.

rangeSummary.value: Native to southern South America. Introduced in Louisiana in the 1930s and spread widely; now in the southeastern and south-central U.S., Oregon, Washington, Maryland and other states, with records in British Columbia.

identification.text: Large semi-aquatic rodent, body 47–61 cm plus a 37–41 cm tail; up to about 9 kg.
Light to dark brown fur; long, round, sparsely haired tail.
Conspicuous white whiskers and prominent incisors on a large, nearly triangular head.
First four toes of the hind feet webbed, the fifth free.
Compared with the beaver: Beavers have a broad flat tail and fully webbed hind feet.
Compared with the muskrat: Muskrats are much smaller with a short side-flattened tail and unwebbed toes.

habitat.text: Fresh marshes preferred, but also bayous, rivers, impoundments, farm ponds, canals, swamps and brackish or salt coastal marshes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal, peaking near midnight; more daytime activity when food is scarce
Digs out roots, rhizomes and tubers with its forepaws, especially in winter; occasionally eats mussels and crustaceans
Feeds in the emergent-vegetation zone of wetlands

resources.title: Polar bear
resources.description: Identify Polar bear, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Polar bear (Ursus maritimus): Very large, stocky bear without the brown bear's shoulder hump. Relatively small head and elongated neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Circumpolar Arctic. In North America, populations occur in western and northern Alaska and the Canadian Arctic archipelago, following the pack ice south in winter.

rangeSummary.value: Circumpolar Arctic. In North America, populations occur in western and northern Alaska and the Canadian Arctic archipelago, following the pack ice south in winter.

identification.text: Very large, stocky bear without the brown bear's shoulder hump.
Relatively small head and elongated neck.
Fur appears white but can look yellowish in summer or brown/grey depending on light; skin is black.
Broad forepaws and furred soles.
Males 300-800 kg and up to 2.5 m long; females 150-300 kg.
Compared with the grizzly (brown) bear: The polar bear lacks the brown bear's shoulder hump and has a smaller head, longer neck and white-appearing coat.

habitat.text: Pack ice of the Arctic Ocean, especially ice edges and pressure ridges; in summer on islands, coasts with landfast ice or stranded on land. Pregnant females den on coasts in winter.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Solitary except females with cubs and mating pairs; bears may gather to scavenge a seal kill.
Mainly still-hunts ringed seals at breathing holes, or stalks seals basking on ice; often eats only the blubber.
Strong swimmer that ranges widely; has been documented as far south as Maine.
Uses a 'chuffing' sound as a greeting; has a keen sense of smell.

conservationStatus.text: The polar bear, wherever found: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2008-05-15.

resources.title: Sika deer
resources.description: Identify Sika deer, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Sika deer (Cervus nippon): Small to medium deer, shoulder height 64-109 cm. Coat chestnut-brown to reddish-olive (varies from yellow-brown to grey or black), marked with seven or eight rows of white spots along the back. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to eastern Asia. Introduced and established in the United States in Maryland, Virginia, Oklahoma, Texas and Wisconsin.

rangeSummary.value: Native to eastern Asia. Introduced and established in the United States in Maryland, Virginia, Oklahoma, Texas and Wisconsin.

identification.text: Small to medium deer, shoulder height 64-109 cm.
Coat chestnut-brown to reddish-olive (varies from yellow-brown to grey or black), marked with seven or eight rows of white spots along the back.
Dark stripe down the middle of the back ending at a large white rump patch that can be flared.
Males only carry narrow, upright antlers with an upswept brow tine, usually 30-66 cm long; in velvet May-August, hard by early September.
Compared with the white-tailed deer: Look for the sika's white-spotted coat, dark stripe down the back ending in a large white rump patch, and the male's narrow, upright antlers.

habitat.text: Primarily forest with a dense understorey, but adapts to freshwater marsh (as in Maryland) and grassland, from sea level to 1,800 m.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Primarily nocturnal and not very gregarious; adult males are solitary most of the year.
Rutting males dig urine-soaked pits with antlers and forefeet and thrash ground cover to mark territory.
Highly vocal: soft whistles, bleats, neighs, and loud screams from males; alarm call a sharp scream, whistle or bark.
Adaptable grazer and browser; good swimmer.

resources.title: Striped skunk
resources.description: Identify Striped skunk, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Striped skunk (Mephitis mephitis): Cat-sized with a stout body, small head, short legs and a long-haired bushy tail; 20-30 in long. Black fur with a thin white stripe down the face and a broad white stripe from the head that forks at the shoulders into two back stripes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: From central Mexico north to the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, and from the Maritimes to west-central British Columbia, across the United States.

rangeSummary.value: From central Mexico north to the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, and from the Maritimes to west-central British Columbia, across the United States.

identification.text: Cat-sized with a stout body, small head, short legs and a long-haired bushy tail; 20-30 in long.
Black fur with a thin white stripe down the face and a broad white stripe from the head that forks at the shoulders into two back stripes.
Stripe pattern varies individually, from nearly absent to covering the whole back.
Long, straight claws for digging.
Compared with the spotted skunks: Spotted skunks are much smaller and marked with several broken white stripes and spots, including a white forehead spot.

habitat.text: Mixed farmland, forest edges, brushy field corners, fencerows and grassy fields broken by wooded ravines, near permanent water; adapts well to people.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal forager; omnivorous, favouring insects (including bee and wasp larvae) in spring and summer, plus mice, other small mammals and carrion.
Warns before spraying by stamping its front feet, raising its tail, growling or hissing; often smelled before seen.
Usually dens in abandoned burrows of woodchucks or foxes, or under stumps, rock piles and buildings.

resources.title: Swamp rabbit
resources.description: Identify Swamp rabbit, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Swamp rabbit (Sylvilagus aquaticus): Largest cottontail, about 1.6-2.7 kg. Ears small relative to other cottontails. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South-central United States and the Gulf Coast, abundant in Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, and also in parts of South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Oklahoma and Missouri. Not found in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: South-central United States and the Gulf Coast, abundant in Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, and also in parts of South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Oklahoma and Missouri. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Largest cottontail, about 1.6-2.7 kg.
Ears small relative to other cottontails.
Head and back a mix of dark brown, rusty brown or black; throat, belly and tail white.
Clear cinnamon-coloured ring around the eye.
Compared with the eastern cottontail: The swamp rabbit is the largest cottontail, with relatively small ears and a clear cinnamon eye-ring.

habitat.text: Swampy lowlands, marshes, floodplains, river tributaries and cypress swamps, usually close to water; rests in depressions in tall grass or leaves.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Most active at dawn, dusk and night; hides motionless by day in hollow logs or dense grass.
Flees in a zig-zag and will enter water, staying still with only its nose above the surface.
Eats grasses, sedges, shrubs, bark, seedlings and twigs.
Usually silent except when threatened; males scent-mark territories.

resources.title: Virginia opossum
resources.description: Identify Virginia opossum, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana): The only marsupial north of Mexico. Long, hairless, prehensile tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Most of the eastern and central U.S. and adjacent southeastern Canada (north into Ontario), west to South Dakota, Colorado and Arizona; introduced on the Pacific coast and into British Columbia, and still expanding north and west.

rangeSummary.value: Most of the eastern and central U.S. and adjacent southeastern Canada (north into Ontario), west to South Dakota, Colorado and Arizona; introduced on the Pacific coast and into British Columbia, and still expanding north and west.

identification.text: The only marsupial north of Mexico.
Long, hairless, prehensile tail.
Whitish underfur tipped with black; coloration varies across the range.
Robust body, short legs and an opposable thumb-like hind toe; about 1.9–2.8 kg.

habitat.text: Varied, from dry country to wet meadows, but prefers woodlands and thickets near water.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Nocturnal and solitary, active dusk to dawn; does not hibernate but is less active in the coldest weather
When threatened adults hiss, bare teeth or flee; feigning death is mostly by young animals
Opportunistic omnivore: small animals, insects, worms, fruit and seeds
Somewhat nomadic, often staying in an area only months

resources.title: White-tailed jackrabbit
resources.description: Identify White-tailed jackrabbit, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: White-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus townsendii): Large hare whose tail is always white (sometimes with a buffy top stripe). Ears rimmed in white and tipped in black year-round. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: West-central Canada and the western and north-central United States: the Great Plains of Alberta and Saskatchewan east to extreme southwestern Ontario and Wisconsin, west to the Rockies and south to central California. The range has contracted in the southeast (e.g., Kansas).

rangeSummary.value: West-central Canada and the western and north-central United States: the Great Plains of Alberta and Saskatchewan east to extreme southwestern Ontario and Wisconsin, west to the Rockies and south to central California. The range has contracted in the southeast (e.g., Kansas).

identification.text: Large hare whose tail is always white (sometimes with a buffy top stripe).
Ears rimmed in white and tipped in black year-round.
Summer upperparts yellowish to grayish brown with white or gray underside.
In snowy northern range turns pure white in winter; farther south only the sides whiten.
Compared with the black-tailed jackrabbit: Black-tailed jackrabbit has a black tail top, black back stripe and black rump patch.
Compared with the snowshoe hare: Snowshoe hare is a smaller forest hare with smaller ears.

habitat.text: Open grasslands, pastures and fields, also forest openings up to alpine tundra, from 40 to 4,300 m.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Nocturnal, feeding sunset to sunrise; rests by day in shallow forms under cover, linked by well-used trails; tunnels into snow in winter.
The least social hare; usually silent but screams if caught.
Eats grasses, forbs and shrubs in summer; shrub bark, alfalfa and winter wheat in winter.

resources.title: Wild boar
resources.description: Identify Wild boar, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Wild boar (Sus scrofa): Hairy, brown, black or gray coat. Long pointed head, narrow snout, upright ears and tusks. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eurasian and North African species. Free-ranging feral swine (wild boar, escaped domestic pigs and hybrids) are reported in at least 35 U.S. states, most commonly in the South, and in Canada mainly in the Prairie Provinces.

rangeSummary.value: Eurasian and North African species. Free-ranging feral swine (wild boar, escaped domestic pigs and hybrids) are reported in at least 35 U.S. states, most commonly in the South, and in Canada mainly in the Prairie Provinces.

identification.text: Hairy, brown, black or gray coat.
Long pointed head, narrow snout, upright ears and tusks.
Long straight tail with a tuft at the tip.
Piglets light brown with tan stripes that fade with age.
Feral domestic pigs and hybrids can look nearly identical; genetics may be needed to tell them apart.
Compared with the feral domestic pig and hybrids: Escaped domestic pigs become hairy and grow tusks; visual separation from wild boar is often impossible.

habitat.text: Extreme habitat generalist: forests, swamps, brushlands, grasslands and farmland, preferring to stay near water.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Lives in family groups called sounders, generally 2–20 animals; adult males often solitary
Breeds from about 6 months old with litters of 2–12, possibly several a year
Roots up the ground while feeding, damaging plants, crops and habitat, and eats ground-nesting birds and other small animals
Quickly learns to avoid people and traps; usually flees rather than fights

resources.title: Wolverine
resources.description: Identify Wolverine, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Wolverine (Gulo gulo): Largest land member of the weasel family, built like a small bear: thick body, short legs, broad head, short ears. Dark brown to black fur with a pale creamy to gold stripe from each shoulder along the flanks to the base of the bushy tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern Canada and Alaska, retaining its range in the Arctic and western mountain and boreal regions but gone from the prairies and much of southeastern Canada; in the contiguous U.S. essentially limited to the mountains of Idaho, Montana, Wyoming and Washington.

rangeSummary.value: Northern Canada and Alaska, retaining its range in the Arctic and western mountain and boreal regions but gone from the prairies and much of southeastern Canada; in the contiguous U.S. essentially limited to the mountains of Idaho, Montana, Wyoming and Washington.

identification.text: Largest land member of the weasel family, built like a small bear: thick body, short legs, broad head, short ears.
Dark brown to black fur with a pale creamy to gold stripe from each shoulder along the flanks to the base of the bushy tail.
White or orange patches common on the throat and chest.
Adult males about 11–18 kg; females 6–12 kg.

habitat.text: Alpine and arctic tundra and boreal and mountain coniferous forest, usually with winter snow cover; in the south limited to large mountain wilderness.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Solitary and wide-ranging; male home ranges can exceed 1,000 km²
Scavenges carrion (often wolf or hunter kills) in winter and hunts small and medium mammals and birds
Marks food and landmarks with urine and musk
Tends to use higher elevations in summer and lower in winter; young are born in snow dens

conservationStatus.text: North American wolverine (Gulo gulo luscus): listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2024-01-02.

resources.title: Woodchuck
resources.description: Identify Woodchuck, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Woodchuck (Marmota monax): Heavy-bodied rodent about 20–26 in long with a short (about 6 in) bristly tail; 5–15 lb. Yellowish-brown to blackish-brown fur with sparse, paler belly hair; dark feet. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: From Oklahoma and Alabama north and northeast through the eastern US, and west across Canada into Alaska.

rangeSummary.value: From Oklahoma and Alabama north and northeast through the eastern US, and west across Canada into Alaska.

identification.text: Heavy-bodied rodent about 20–26 in long with a short (about 6 in) bristly tail; 5–15 lb.
Yellowish-brown to blackish-brown fur with sparse, paler belly hair; dark feet.
Broad, chisel-shaped white front incisors.

habitat.text: Open fields, meadows, pastures, fencerows and woodland edges, preferring well-drained slopes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Active in early morning and late evening in summer.
Sharp alarm whistle; 'chuck-chuck' sounds while feeding.
Digs burrows with a main entrance marked by a dirt mound and inconspicuous back exits.
Hibernates from about October to early spring; eats grasses, clover, alfalfa, dandelion and crops.
